T3_nbs_hazard_farming.mitigation_mechanism: Tree canopies reduce evapotranspiration from crop and soil surfaces through shading, lower temperatures under canopy by 2–5°C, and improve soil water retention via increased organic matter and macropore structure from root channels. Hydraulic lift by deep-rooted trees moves water from moist subsoil to drier upper layers, maintaining moisture availability to interplanted crops during dry spells.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Mitigation effect requires canopy closure; limited in first 2–3 years post-establishment. In extreme arid zones (AI <0.2), tree water demand can compete with crops and reduce overall system productivity unless drought-tolerant species are selected.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.justification: Brandt et al. (2015) identify agroforestry as a top-priority CSA practice for drought-prone mixed rainfed systems in East Africa. Ahmad et al. (2020) demonstrate high land potential for agroforestry in South Asian rainfed systems where drought is the primary climate barrier. Mendonça et al. (2022) map agroforestry as a high-priority drought adaptation practice in Brazilian rain-fed landscapes.

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.mitigation_mechanism: Parkland agroforestry (e.g., Faidherbia albida, Vitellaria paradoxa) is a traditional drought adaptation strategy in Sahelian and sub-Saharan agropastoral systems. Retained trees provide nitrogen fixation, organic matter, shade, and fodder during dry seasons. Farmer-managed natural regeneration (FMNR) of parkland trees has demonstrably increased crop yields under rainfall stress.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Species selection critical — reverse-phenology trees (e.g., Faidherbia) that shed leaves during growing season are most compatible with crops. Requires tenure security for farmers to invest in tree retention.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.justification: Haile (2024) demonstrates parkland agroforestry as the most suitable NbS for semi-arid agropastoral zones in Ethiopia. Brandt et al. (2015) confirm agroforestry priority in drought-exposed Turkana and Wajir counties (arid agropastoral). Ahmad & Goparaju (2017) show high agroforestry suitability in Jharkhand dryland zones.

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.mitigation_mechanism: Riparian buffer strips and waterway-adjacent agroforestry systems reduce peak runoff by intercepting rainfall, increasing infiltration, and stabilising streambanks. Root systems of perennial trees increase soil macroporosity and infiltration rates. Windbreak and alley cropping systems slow surface water flow across slopes, reducing runoff velocity and peak discharge at watershed scale.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Effect on peak flood discharge is meaningful only at catchment scale with significant landscape coverage (>20–30% of watershed area). Poorly designed systems in floodplains can increase risk during extreme events. Castle et al. (2025) flag floodplain areas as unsuitable for agroforestry siting due to structural damage risk.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.justification: Baldwin et al. (2022) demonstrate integrated agroforestry and FloodWise practices (dry dams, riparian buffers) for flood mitigation in North Carolina, using spatial optimisation to site systems away from high-hazard floodplains. Castle et al. (2025) include riparian buffers as flood-risk-reducing agroforestry sub-practice. Ahmad et al. (2020) map agroforestry co-benefit for flood adaptation in South Asian peri-urban landscapes.

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.mitigation_mechanism: Tree canopy within or adjacent to paddy systems reduces air and soil surface temperatures through shading and evapotranspiration, creating cooler microclimates. Shade trees reduce heat stress on workers and livestock. Fruit and timber trees in paddy bunds provide income diversification buffering climate-induced crop yield losses.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Dense shading reduces paddy yields; optimal tree density and placement must avoid excessive shading of rice crop. Effect strongest in regions with heat index regularly exceeding 35°C. Literature evidence is primarily from South and Southeast Asia.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.justification: Ahmad et al. (2018) assess agroforestry suitability in Bihar including irrigated areas. Nath et al. (2021) include irrigated zones in Eastern Himalayan agroforestry suitability mapping where heat stress in lower elevation farming systems is a growing concern under climate change.

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.mitigation_mechanism: Tree canopy provides direct cooling of crop microclimate, reducing soil surface temperatures by up to 10°C and ambient air temperatures by 2–5°C. Shading reduces evaporative stress on annual crops. Shade provision for livestock prevents heat-induced productivity and mortality losses in silvo-pastoral systems.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Species selection must balance shade provision with crop light requirements. Effect limited in early establishment phase.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.justification: Yadav et al. (2024) explicitly model temperature stress layers (Tmax_May, Tmax_Jan) as key agroforestry suitability and hazard variables in Punjab. Kiziridis et al. (2026) map silvopastoral systems in Spain and Greece partly in response to increasing heat stress on open pasture systems.

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.mitigation_mechanism: Silvopastoral agroforestry systems can reduce fire spread through management of grass fuel loads by grazing and by creating heterogeneous fire breaks. However, woody biomass accumulation in poorly managed systems can increase fire intensity. Fire risk management depends critically on species selection and stocking rates.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Poorly managed agroforestry systems with dense woody understorey and dry grass accumulation can INCREASE fire risk in savanna/dry forest contexts. Yadav et al. (2024) explicitly include wildfire susceptibility as a constraint layer, excluding high-fire-risk areas from agroforestry prioritisation. Context-specific species selection (non-flammable vs. resinous species) is critical.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.justification: Yadav et al. (2024) model wildfire susceptibility as a suitability constraint, treating high fire risk areas as hazard barriers to agroforestry. Nath et al. (2021) note fire risk as a spatial exclusion criterion in fire-prone parts of the Eastern Himalayas. Kiziridis et al. (2026) consider silvopastoral systems in fire-prone Mediterranean contexts where fire risk is a design constraint.

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.mitigation_mechanism: Deep-rooted trees increase soil water extraction and drainage through root channels and macropore formation. Trees on terraces and bunds in highland systems stabilise slopes and reduce surface waterlogging. Agroforestry systems with well-drained soils on sloped terrain naturally shed excess water more effectively than flat monocultures.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: In very poorly drained soils or flatland systems, trees may not provide drainage benefit and some species may not tolerate waterlogged conditions. Soil drainage class is a key suitability determinant (Wotlolan et al. 2021, Haris et al. 2021).
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.justification: Wotlolan et al. (2021) include drainage as a key suitability criterion for agroforestry in Fiji highlands. Mushtaq et al. (2023) include soil drainage class as a suitability variable for mulberry agroforestry in Himalayan Kashmir. Seja et al. (2022) map drainage as a land suitability criterion for agroforestry allocation in Tanzania.

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.mitigation_mechanism: In existing tree crop systems (cocoa, coffee, oil palm), diversification with additional multi-purpose trees creates a layered canopy providing mutual shade, humidity retention, and microclimate buffering. Shade-grown coffee and cacao agroforestry systems show greater resilience to drought years than monocultures through reduced evaporative demand.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Species must be compatible with existing plantation crop. Farmer uptake requires clear economic co-benefits to justify canopy management costs.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.justification: Singh et al. (2024) identify tree crop systems as a key context for scaling agroforestry using remote sensing to map adoption potential. Palma et al. (2007) demonstrate economic and environmental co-benefits of silvoarable systems in European tree crop contexts.

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.mitigation_mechanism: Windbreaks reduce wind velocity downstream for distances up to 15-20 times the height of the shelterbelt, mitigating wind-induced soil erosion and protecting crops from lodging.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Requires strategic spacing and layout; selection of species that do not compete heavily with interplanted crops.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.justification: Cleugh (1998) shows that windbreaks shelter crops from mechanical wind stress, reducing wind speeds by 20-50%. Sudmeyer et al. (2004) confirm yield increases in wind-sheltered zones.

context_overrides.note: Context-specific evidence (ev_slope_nath21, ev_slope_mendonca22, ev_slope_mendonca23, ev_slope_haris21, ev_slope_wotlolan21, ev_slope_chuma21).

Land cover is an eligibility filter, not a graduated suitability variable. Cropland (class 40) and grassland/pasture (20, 30) are the primary targets for agroforestry integration. Built-up, water, ice, and mangroves are hard exclusions. Used as the primary land-use mask in Ahmad et al. (2020), Castle et al. (2025), Baldwin et al. (2022), and the majority of stocktake papers.

Strict nature reserves (IUCN I–II) prohibit agricultural intervention including agroforestry. Hard exclusion required regardless of biophysical suitability. Chuma et al. (2021) use the Itombwe Nature Reserve boundary as a hard exclusion layer in DR Congo agroforestry suitability mapping. Pinto et al. (2019) use protected area boundaries as planning zones in Montado conservation prioritisation.

T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Agroforestry diversifies farm income through timber, fruit, fodder, and non-timber forest products, and can provide direct dietary benefits from edible trees. Income diversification buffers against crop failure events and reduces seasonal food insecurity. Long-term carbon revenue streams (where accessible) can provide additional cash income to smallholders.
T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Poverty reduction effect is conditional on functional market access for agroforestry products and sufficient farm size to absorb tree integration without reducing food crop area below subsistence thresholds. Tenure security required for smallholders to invest in long-rotation tree crops.

economic_value_range.source_note: Wide range reflects variation from subsistence parkland systems (~$50/ha/yr in additional income) to intensively managed silvoarable or carbon-credited systems (~$500/ha/yr). Marinis et al. (2022) report NPV of CAD $1.186 billion at landscape scale. Palma et al. (2007) demonstrate positive iNPV for European silvoarable systems.

T6_nbs_scorecard.justification: Ahmad & Goparaju (2017) position agroforestry explicitly as a livelihood improvement and poverty reduction strategy in Jharkhand, India. Brandt et al. (2015) identify agroforestry as a CSA practice that directly targets food security and income stability in Kenya's poorest counties. [archetype: Long horizon archetype: 5–15 years to positive net cashflow; patient capital, carbon finance, or output-based aid required during establishment phase. CrossBoundary classification: long_horizon.]

T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Trees in agroforestry systems sequester carbon in aboveground biomass (stem, branches, leaves) and belowground (roots). Agroforestry also improves soil organic carbon through litter inputs, root turnover, and reduced tillage frequency. Compared to open cropland, agroforestry systems store 2–5× more carbon per hectare in mature states.
T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Carbon sequestration rates vary widely by species, climate, soil, and management. High rates apply only after canopy closure (typically 5–10 years post-establishment). Permanence requires long-term tree retention and management.

economic_value_range.source_note: Based on sequestration rates of 1–10 t CO₂/ha/yr × carbon price of $10–30/t. Kiziridis et al. (2026) map silvopastoral carbon sequestration potential for climate policy. Mendonça et al. (2023) use SOC sequestration potential as the primary prioritisation criterion.

T6_nbs_scorecard.justification: Kiziridis et al. (2026) explicitly optimise agroforestry siting to maximise carbon sequestration in Spain and Greece. Mendonça et al. (2023) use SOC sequestration as the leading environmental criterion for prioritising agroforestry areas in Brazil. Palma et al. (2007) demonstrate carbon sequestration as a primary environmental performance metric for European silvoarable systems. [archetype: Carbon revenue streams begin only after MRV verification (typically 3–5 years post-establishment). Carbon finance requires upfront technical assistance costs of $50–200/ha. Most viable for large-scale aggregated schemes.]

T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Agroforestry diversifies farm output to include fruits, nuts, fodder, and fuelwood alongside staple crops, reducing household food insecurity. Tree shade moderates heat stress on crops, and improved soil organic matter from leaf litter increases long-term soil fertility and yield stability. In drought years, deep-rooted trees can maintain partial productivity while annual crops fail.
T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Food security benefit requires that tree integration does not compete excessively with food crops for light and water, especially during crop establishment. Compatible species pairing and appropriate tree density are critical. Effect may be negative in the short term (1–3 years) if tree establishment reduces crop area.
T6_nbs_scorecard.justification: Brandt et al. (2015) identify food security improvement as the primary CSA outcome targeted by agroforestry in East Africa. Ahmad et al. (2020) frame the South Asia agroforestry scale-up explicitly around food security and climate resilience co-benefits. [v0.3.0 reroute: food_security_risk → production_gap per T5 ratification (issue #34); see methodology/opportunity_space_T5.md.]

T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Agroforestry introduces structural complexity and functional diversity into agricultural landscapes, creating habitat for invertebrates, birds, and small mammals. Tree species diversity in agroforestry systems supports pollinator communities and pest-control predators. Riparian and corridor agroforestry enables connectivity between fragmented natural habitat patches.
T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Biodiversity benefit requires diverse tree species selection (not monoculture timber plantations). Greatest benefit in landscapes highly degraded by intensive monoculture agriculture with little remaining natural habitat. Effect may be limited near intact natural forests where conversion to agroforestry could reduce habitat quality.
T6_nbs_scorecard.justification: Pinto et al. (2019) demonstrate agroforestry (Montado) as the primary biodiversity conservation vehicle in Portugal's agricultural landscapes, using spatial prioritisation to identify high-value agroforestry zones. Chuma et al. (2021) site agroforestry in the buffer zone of the Itombwe Reserve to support wildlife habitat connectivity. Nath et al. (2021) include biodiversity indicators in the Eastern Himalayan agroforestry suitability framework.

T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Tree root systems bind soil and increase macroporosity, reducing surface runoff and water erosion. Leaf litter and organic matter inputs increase soil organic carbon, improving soil structure, water retention, and fertility. Windbreak and shelterbelt agroforestry systems reduce wind erosion. Nitrogen-fixing trees (Leucaena, Faidherbia, Gliricidia) improve soil nitrogen status, reducing fertiliser dependency.
T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Soil protection effect requires established canopy and functioning root systems (typically 3–7 years post-establishment). Effect may be delayed or limited in very degraded, compacted, or saline soils that require additional soil rehabilitation inputs.

economic_value_range.source_note: Avoided fertiliser costs and soil remediation costs. Castle et al. (2025) use soil erosion reduction (GloSEM model) as a primary agroforestry co-benefit. Palma et al. (2007) include nitrate leaching reduction and erosion control in European silvoarable economic assessment.

T6_nbs_scorecard.justification: Castle et al. (2025) prioritise agroforestry in areas with high water and wind erosion risk as the primary targeting criterion. Palma et al. (2007) demonstrate significant reduction in soil erosion (RUSLE) and nitrate leaching as environmental performance metrics. Mendonça et al. (2022, 2023) include soil organic carbon and slope stability as priority criteria. [archetype: Soil improvement benefits compound over time; economic value realised through reduced input costs and sustained yield maintenance over decades.]

T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Agroforestry tree canopy reduces evapotranspiration from crop and soil surfaces, lowers ambient temperature by 2–5°C under canopy, and hydraulic lift by deep-rooted trees moves subsoil water to upper layers. Combined effects maintain soil moisture during dry spells and reduce crop heat stress. Parkland agroforestry in semi-arid Sahel shows 20–80% higher crop yields under drought conditions compared to open fields.
T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Drought mitigation effect strongest in semi-arid to sub-humid contexts (AI 0.3–0.65). In humid zones, drought is less limiting so the marginal benefit is smaller. Effect requires established trees (3–7 years establishment).
T6_nbs_scorecard.justification: Brandt et al. (2015) demonstrate agroforestry as the top-ranked CSA practice for drought mitigation in East Africa's dryland farming systems. Mendonça et al. (2022) map agroforestry as a high-priority drought adaptation measure in Brazil. Ahmad et al. (2020) quantify land potential for scaling agroforestry in South Asia specifically in drought-exposed rainfed systems.

T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Agroforestry establishment requires upfront investment in planting material (seedlings), labour for planting, establishment maintenance, and often fencing or protection from livestock browsing. Costs are higher for intensively managed silvoarable systems compared to low-input parkland or FMNR systems.
T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Establishment cost is highly variable: FMNR and farmer-managed regeneration systems have near-zero direct costs. High-value commercial silvoarable systems (walnut, oak, fruit trees) have establishment costs of $500–1500/ha. Subsidies, carbon finance, or output-based aid can offset establishment costs.

economic_value_range.source_note: Low end: FMNR systems with minimal planting material cost. High end: intensively managed commercial silvoarable systems in Europe (Palma et al. 2007). Marinis et al. (2022) report detailed NPV calculations including silviculture costs for DR Congo context.

T6_nbs_scorecard.justification: Baldwin et al. (2022) build an explicit habitat creation cost surface to optimise agroforestry siting under budget constraints. Unger & Lakes (2023) quantify implementation cost savings between natural regeneration and active tree planting. Marinis et al. (2022) calculate full NPV including silviculture costs. [archetype: CrossBoundary long_horizon archetype: large upfront establishment costs with returns deferred 5–15 years. Requires patient capital, output-based aid, or advance carbon credit payments to bridge establishment financing gap.]

T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Proximity to road networks and markets enables farmers to access seedlings, technical inputs, and extension services for agroforestry establishment, and to sell timber, fruit, and non-timber forest products at commercially viable prices. Market access is a key determinant of whether agroforestry investment generates returns sufficient to justify the long payback period.
T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Market access effect is strongest for commercial agroforestry sub-types (timber, fruits). Subsistence-oriented parkland agroforestry is less sensitive to road access. Effect is strongly context-dependent: carbon credit access is less dependent on road proximity than timber markets.
T6_nbs_scorecard.justification: Chuma et al. (2021) include road access distance as an explicit suitability criterion, recognising market access as a key system constraint. Castle et al. (2025) include infrastructure connectivity as a social-ecological suitability layer. Brandt et al. (2015) identify market linkages as a key enabling condition for CSA/agroforestry uptake in East Africa. [archetype: Market access is a prerequisite for commercial viability of long-horizon investments. Without market linkages, agroforestry remains subsistence-scale and carbon credit participation is unlikely.]

T0_nbs_registry.description_short: Re-establishment or protection of forest/tree cover on degraded, deforested or non-forest land, spanning the restoration continuum from passive natural regeneration through assisted regeneration to active planting.
T0_nbs_registry.description_technical: Forest restoration re-establishes forest structure, composition and function on degraded or deforested land. Suitability is reasoned along the restoration continuum: passive natural regeneration (recovery after pressure removal, gated by regeneration potential — seed-source proximity, residual cover, low disturbance), assisted natural regeneration (barrier removal + management where regeneration potential is partial), and active planting (reforestation/afforestation/enrichment, gated by the planting envelope for target species where natural regeneration will not deliver). Coastal mangrove restoration (distinct coastal-hydrology driver) and forest protection/CBFM (existing standing forest x threat x governance) are registered but parked pending scope sign-off. Distinct from agroforestry regeneration-on-farmland (on-farm vs forest/non-farm land).

upfront_cost_usd_ha.source_note: Wide range: assisted/natural regeneration low (~$100-600/ha) vs active planting/afforestation high (~$1000-3000/ha). Scoping-grade indicative, not CBA.

primary_references: Chazdon (2008) - Beyond deforestation: restoring forests and ecosystem services on degraded lands
Crouzeilles et al. (2016) - A global meta-analysis on the ecological drivers of forest restoration success
Holl & Aerts (2011) - When and where to actively restore ecosystems?
Strassburg et al. (2020) - Global priority areas for ecosystem restoration
Chazdon & Guariguata (2016) - Natural regeneration as a tool for large-scale forest restoration in the tropics
Stanturf et al. (2014) - Contemporary forest restoration: a review emphasizing function

T0_nbs_registry.description_short: Vegetated strips (grass and/or woody) along watercourses that intercept sediment/nutrients, stabilise banks, shade streams and provide habitat; established by planting or by protecting/restoring natural riparian vegetation.
T0_nbs_registry.description_technical: Riparian buffers are linear NbS placed along the watercourse network. Suitability is reasoned per establishment driver: F1 planted buffers (grass/herbaceous filter strips or woody/forested buffers) gated by watercourse proximity, riparian slope/width, adjacent-land runoff load and the planting envelope; F2 natural/restored riparian vegetation gated by existing riparian condition / regeneration potential and hydro-connectivity. Footprint is zonal_linear (buffer length per stream-km, never pixel area). Floodplain/hydro-reconnection is registered but parked pending a river-restoration scope call. Distinct from agroforestry linear plantings (windbreaks/contour buffers), which are gated by wind/slope-flow on farmland, not the watercourse network.

upfront_cost_usd_ha.source_note: Grass strips low; planted woody buffers higher. Scoping-grade indicative, not CBA.

primary_references: Mayer et al. (2007) - Meta-analysis of nitrogen removal in riparian buffers
Zhang et al. (2010) - Buffer width and pollutant removal
Stutter et al. (2019) - Riparian buffer management
Sweeney & Newbold (2014) - Buffer width for stream ecological protection

T0_nbs_registry.description_short: Deliberate capture, storage, and managed use of surface runoff and rainwater through structural and land-based interventions to improve agricultural water availability, recharge groundwater, and reduce erosion and flood risk.
T0_nbs_registry.description_technical: Water harvesting and conservation encompasses interventions that intercept, retain, and store precipitation and surface runoff for productive use or groundwater recharge. Structural sub-practices include check dams, farm ponds, percolation tanks, gully plugs, earthen and small dams, and cisterns. Land-based sub-practices include contour bunding, terracing, tied ridging, contour trenching, and micro-catchment systems. Site selection is determined primarily by slope, drainage morphology, runoff potential (SCS Curve Number), soil texture, and rainfall. The dominant spatial method across 85 stocktake papers is GIS-based multi-criteria evaluation (MCE) using AHP-weighted overlay validated against DEM-derived hydrological parameters.

upfront_cost_usd_ha.source_note: Low end: simple contour bunds at community labour cost (~$50/ha). High end: engineered check dams or lined farm ponds (~$800/ha). Teréncio et al. (2017) calculate EUR/m3 storage cost ratios. Ibrahim et al. (2019) apply cost-minimisation in dam site selection. Ahmed et al. (2023) monetise ecosystem-service benefits in USD.

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.mitigation_mechanism: Farm ponds, check dams, and percolation tanks capture seasonal rainfall for use during dry spells, extending the growing season and providing supplemental irrigation at critical crop growth stages. Contour bunds retain in-situ soil moisture, reducing crop stress during within-season dry periods.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Effectiveness constrained by storage capacity vs catchment area. Sediment management essential — siltation can reduce storage by 20-40% within 5 years without desiltation.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.justification: Jha et al. (2014), Singh et al. (2016), Bera & Mukhopadhyay (2023) and the majority of the 85 WH stocktake papers address mixed rainfed systems in South Asia and Africa where drought is the primary water stress.

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.mitigation_mechanism: In semi-arid systems with 300-700mm rainfall concentrated in 2-4 months, water harvesting is the dominant strategy. Check dams, gully plugs, and micro-watershed systems harvest flash runoff. Groundwater recharge from percolation tanks sustains livestock watering through the 7-9 month dry season.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Flash runoff events are highly variable — design standards must account for inter-annual variability. Structures sized for mean rainfall will overflow in high-rainfall years and be insufficient in low-rainfall years.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.justification: Haile & Suryabhagavan (2018), Mahmoud et al. (2014), Mbilinyi et al. (2007), and Zheng et al. (2023) all address semi-arid agropastoral contexts in Africa and Asia where water harvesting is the primary livelihood resilience strategy.

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.mitigation_mechanism: Check dams and farm ponds intercept peak runoff flows, reducing volume and velocity reaching downstream channels. Contour bunds and bench terraces slow surface flow, extending time of concentration and reducing peak discharge. At watershed scale, a structure network can attenuate flood peaks by 20-40% for moderate-frequency events.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Effect on extreme flood events (>50-year return period) is limited. Structures designed for WH are too small to meaningfully attenuate catastrophic floods. Poorly sited structures that overtop can increase downstream risk. Terencio et al. (2017) flag floodplain locations as hazardous for RWH.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.justification: Abd-el-Kader et al. (2023), Ahmad et al. (2024), and Al-Hasani et al. (2023) explicitly target flood risk reduction as a RWH co-benefit.

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.mitigation_mechanism: Bench terraces and contour bunds retain rainfall in-situ on sloped highland terrain, dramatically reducing surface runoff and increasing soil moisture. Hillside ponds and check dams in valley bottoms capture dry-season flows for supplemental irrigation of high-value vegetable crops.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Terracing is labour-intensive to construct and maintain. Terrace failure due to burrowing animals or storm events can cause severe erosion. Slope angle is a hard constraint — terracing above 45 degrees is unsafe and uneconomic.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.justification: Kumar et al. (2018) demonstrate morphometric analysis for WH structure siting in the Himalayan Lower Kosi basin. Amdihun et al. (2014) and Worku et al. (2020) cover Ethiopian highlands. Jhariya et al. (2018) prioritise highland watershed management.

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.mitigation_mechanism: Small reservoirs, pans, and earth dams in pastoral landscapes store seasonal rainfall for livestock watering throughout the dry season. Groundwater recharge from percolation tanks sustains boreholes and hand pumps. Strategic placement along seasonal watercourses maximises capture of flash runoff events.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Large communal water points can concentrate livestock, causing overgrazing and degradation around structures. Governance arrangements for communal water points are critical to sustainability.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.justification: Mahmoud et al. (2014) map RWH potential in Somali and Borena pastoral regions. Mbilinyi et al. (2007) and Haile & Suryabhagavan (2018) cover pastoral contexts in Tanzania and Ethiopia. Shalamzari et al. (2019) address RWH for wildlife and livestock.

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.mitigation_mechanism: Gully plugs and check dams intercept surface runoff before it concentrates in low-lying areas, reducing waterlogging in valley bottoms. Where siting accounts for drainage patterns, structures can intercept runoff before it inundates cropland.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Waterlogging mitigation is highly dependent on precise siting relative to drainage topology. Structures in naturally waterlogged floodplain areas risk failure. This application is secondary to drought mitigation in most stocktake papers.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.justification: Several stocktake papers include waterlogging risk as a siting constraint. Terencio et al. (2017) flag flood/waterlogging risk as a suitability constraint. Indirect evidence from watershed management literature.

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.mitigation_mechanism: Water stored in farm ponds from RWH can supplement canal irrigation during heat stress periods when evapotranspirative demand peaks. The primary relationship is indirect — stored water reduces temperature stress by maintaining adequate soil moisture, not by directly cooling crops.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Direct heat stress mitigation from RWH is limited. Primary benefit is maintaining water supply reliability. Paddy systems are typically water-sufficient; RWH value is greatest at the tail end of irrigation schemes.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.justification: Indirect evidence from South Asian paddy contexts. Not directly addressed as a heat stress intervention in the 85 WH stocktake papers — rated from expert opinion.

T3_nbs_hazard_farming.mitigation_mechanism: Water harvesting structures do not directly address fire risk in dryland cereal systems. There is no mechanistic pathway by which check dams or farm ponds reduce wildfire ignition or spread at landscape scale.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.caveats: Fire risk management requires fuel management approaches. Including fire as a benefit of RWH would misrepresent the evidence base.
T3_nbs_hazard_farming.justification: No papers in the 85-paper WH stocktake identified fire mitigation as a benefit of water harvesting and conservation. This none rating reflects absence of evidence.

context_overrides.note: Terracing and bench terraces are viable at steeper slopes in highlands where they are traditional practice (Krois & Schulte 2014, Amdihun et al. 2014)
In arid zones, very gentle slopes needed to capture scarce runoff efficiently; steeper slopes generate flash flows that exceed storage capacity (Adham et al. 2018, Hassan et al. 2025)

T4_suitability_mappings.justification: Slope is the single most frequently used input variable across all 85 WH stocktake papers (72 of 85). The 1-8 degree optimal range reflects the consensus across Bera & Mukhopadhyay (2023), Alene et al. (2022), Hassan et al. (2025), Jha et al. (2014), Vema et al. (2019), and Zheng et al. (2023). Slopes < 1 degree risk waterlogging and structural foundation issues; slopes > 30 degrees are unsafe for dam/bund construction and generate erosive flash runoff.

context_overrides.note: Semi-arid optimal range lower — this is where WH provides highest marginal benefit (Mahmoud et al. 2014, Alene et al. 2022)
In humid tropics, WH targets excess seasonal runoff; optimal range shifts higher (Umugwaneza et al. 2022)

T4_suitability_mappings.justification: Rainfall (38 of 85 papers) directly determines runoff volume available for capture. Below 100mm, runoff is insufficient for most structural WH. Above 1800mm, natural water availability reduces WH investment need. The 250-800mm optimal range corresponds to semi-arid and sub-humid zones where water scarcity is acute but rainfall is sufficient to generate meaningful runoff. Used in SCS-CN calculations across virtually all quantitative WH papers.

class_labels.D: Clayey — very slow infiltration, high runoff, good pond seepage resistance

T4_suitability_mappings.justification: Soil texture (27 of 85 papers) determines both runoff generation potential (HSG A = low runoff, D = high runoff) and pond/dam seepage integrity. Higher-class HSG soils generate more runoff suitable for capture and are better at retaining stored water. Vema et al. (2019) use soil permeability as one of three core fuzzy inference inputs. Jha et al. (2014), Singh et al. (2016), and Bera & Mukhopadhyay (2023) all use soil texture/HSG in AHP-weighted MCDA.

Drainage density (21 of 85 papers) indicates runoff concentration potential and stream network density. Moderate drainage density (0.5-3 km/km2) indicates sufficient surface flow to sustain check dams and percolation tanks. Very low drainage density (< 0.5) suggests insufficient runoff; very high density (> 6) indicates highly erosive landscape unsuitable for stable structure siting. Used by Kumar et al. (2018), Bera & Mukhopadhyay (2023), Singh et al. (2016), and Jha et al. (2014).

Stream order (14 of 85 papers) is a key discriminator for WH structure type and scale. First- and second-order streams are optimal for check dams and gully plugs; third-order for percolation tanks; fourth-order for farm ponds and small dams. Kumar et al. (2018), Singh et al. (2016), Alene et al. (2022), and Hassan et al. (2025) all include stream order as a primary MCDA suitability criterion.

Land cover determines the CN value for runoff estimation and the land-use compatibility of WH structure siting. Grassland and shrubland generate reliable runoff and allow construction without crop displacement. Built-up, permanent water, snow, and mangroves are hard exclusions. Used across the majority of WH stocktake papers as the LULC input to CN calculation.

Construction of WH structures in strict nature reserves (IUCN Cat I-II) is prohibited. Hard exclusion regardless of biophysical suitability. Applied across all papers that include protected area layers as exclusion zones.

context_overrides.note: In semi-arid contexts, WH structures can be built with local labour at greater distances from roads; threshold relaxed relative to global default

T4_suitability_mappings.scenario_description: Removes road access as a construction constraint, revealing the additional WH opportunity space that would become viable with road infrastructure investment. Relevant for project design decisions about complementary road investments.
T4_suitability_mappings.justification: Road proximity is less critical for WH than for agroforestry, as many WH structures can be built with local labour and simple equipment. However, larger structures (check dams, farm ponds with liners) require material transport. Threshold set at 5km (suitable) to 25km (unsuitable) reflecting typical tractor/cart reach in rural settings. Weight deliberately low.

Areas with > 80% permanent water occurrence (rivers, lakes, perennial ponds) are not candidates for new WH structure siting — they are already saturated or represent natural water bodies. Hard exclusion. Al-Hasani et al. (2023, 2025) and multiple Iraqi/Middle East papers incorporate existing water body layers as exclusion zones.

T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: WH structures increase agricultural water availability, enabling crop intensification and expanding the cropping season. This directly increases farm income and food production for poor smallholders. In pastoral systems, livestock watering points reduce dry-season livestock mortality, protecting household assets. Benefits are realised quickly (1-3 years) compared to tree-based NbS.
T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Poverty reduction effect requires that farmers have secure land tenure to invest in structure maintenance and can access markets for surplus production enabled by improved water. Social equity dimensions (who controls pond access) need explicit attention.

economic_value_range.source_note: Low: subsistence-scale water availability improvement from gully plugs and bunds (~$30/ha/yr income equivalent). High: farm pond enabling double-cropping or high-value horticulture (~$400/ha/yr). Ahmed et al. (2023) monetise crop pollination and forage production benefits in USD. Terencio et al. (2017) calculate investment cost ratios in EUR/m3 storage.

T6_nbs_scorecard.justification: Shadeed et al. (2019) explicitly construct a water poverty index and WH suitability map, confirming WH is most valuable in high water-poverty areas. Mahmoud et al. (2014) target the poorest drought-prone zones for RWH in Ethiopia. [archetype: Quick_returns archetype: construction costs recovered within 1-3 seasons from improved yield stability and expanded irrigation. Most accessible economic archetype for poor smallholders without access to patient capital.]

T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: WH structures directly bridge the gap between crop water demand and rainfall supply. Farm ponds store wet-season runoff for dry-season irrigation. Check dams raise groundwater tables, enabling dry-season cropping from wells. Contour bunding and tied ridging retain in-situ soil moisture, extending effective growing season and reducing yield gaps from mid-season dry spells.
T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Effect proportional to storage volume relative to command area. Requires functional distribution infrastructure (pipes, canals) for stored water to reach crops. Evaporation losses (up to 30-50% in hot arid environments) reduce effective storage. Harka et al. (2020) explicitly model evaporation as a barrier in arid contexts.

economic_value_range.source_note: Range reflects value of water made available: from subsistence supplemental irrigation to commercial horticulture. Terencio et al. (2017) calculate EUR/m3 storage and irrigation benefit ratios.

T6_nbs_scorecard.justification: This is the fundamental purpose of water harvesting investment. Confirmed across all 85 stocktake papers as the primary intended outcome. Quantified by Singh et al. (2016), Alene et al. (2022), and Bera & Mukhopadhyay (2023) through runoff potential and demand matching analysis. [archetype: This is the core economic driver for WH investment — direct crop production value from water made available.]

T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Check dams and gully plugs trap sediment, reducing soil loss from active gullies. Contour bunding and terracing break slope length, reducing erosive runoff velocity and soil detachment. Percolation tanks increase infiltration, reducing surface flow erosive power. WH structures collectively shift the water balance from erosive surface flow toward storage and infiltration.
T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Sediment trapping requires periodic de-silting to maintain storage capacity; neglected structures lose function within 5-10 years. Terracing effectiveness depends on correct bund height and spacing for local slope and rainfall intensity.

economic_value_range.source_note: Avoided soil loss valued at replacement fertiliser cost. Singh et al. (2023) quantify RUSLE-based soil loss and watershed prioritisation. Al-Shamiri & Ziadat (2012) conduct monetary cost-benefit analysis of erosion control through WH.

T6_nbs_scorecard.justification: Singh et al. (2023) explicitly apply RUSLE modelling to prioritise WH sites for soil loss prevention. Zhang et al. (2020) use multi-criteria decision analysis including erosion to identify SWC priority areas in China. Al-Shamiri & Ziadat (2012) monetise the erosion control benefit of WH in Yemen. [archetype: Soil conservation benefits compound over time — soils that erode are lost permanently; prevention costs far less than rehabilitation.]

T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: Percolation tanks, check dams, and farm ponds in high-recharge-potential zones allow stored surface water to percolate into shallow aquifers, raising groundwater tables. This sustains dry-season well and spring yields, providing water for livestock and domestic use beyond the direct irrigation command area. Recharge benefits extend spatially beyond the structure footprint.
T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Recharge effect requires permeable geology and favourable soil conditions. Clay-rich formations or impermeable bedrock limit subsurface recharge despite surface storage. Mussa et al. (2020) map groundwater recharge zones specifically to target percolation tank placement.
T6_nbs_scorecard.justification: Singh et al. (2016) identify prospective sites specifically for water harvesting and artificial groundwater recharge as combined objectives. Mussa et al. (2020) use hydrogeological delineation to prioritise recharge zones. Jha et al. (2014) include percolation tank siting explicitly for groundwater recharge. [v0.3.0 reroute: groundwater_recharge_potential → water_stress per T5 ratification (issue #34); see methodology/opportunity_space_T5.md.]

T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: WH structures convert episodic rainfall into stored water accessible during dry spells and drought years. Farm ponds, check dams, and cisterns provide 30-90 days of additional water supply beyond the rainy season. In drought years, stored water can sustain minimum crop production or livestock survival where rain-dependent farming would fail completely. This is the primary climate adaptation function of the NbS.
T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Drought mitigation proportional to storage volume relative to command area water demand. Multi-year droughts can exhaust storage. Evaporation losses (especially in hot, windy arid environments) can reach 30-50% of stored volume. Maximum benefit in semi-arid zones (MAP 250-600mm) where drought is frequent but rainfall is sufficient to fill storage.
T6_nbs_scorecard.justification: This is the primary climate benefit of WH — confirmed across the vast majority of all 85 stocktake papers. hc et al. (2020) prioritise WH ponds specifically for drought from climate variability. Mahmoud et al. (2014) target the drought-prone Somali and Borena zones. Buraihi & Shariff (2015) assess future drought risk scenarios to justify WH site selection.

T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: WH structures intercept and store surface runoff that would otherwise contribute to downstream flooding. Check dams and contour bunds slow peak flow velocity and extend travel time, reducing downstream flood peaks. Landscape-scale WH investment can meaningfully reduce flash flood risk in small to medium watersheds. However, overtopped or failed structures can temporarily increase flood risk.
T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Flood mitigation effect requires landscape-scale deployment; individual structures have negligible effect on major flood events. Structure siting must avoid floodplain positions where inundation would damage or overtop them. Al-Hasani et al. (2023) model flood regulation as an explicit ecosystem-service output of WH.
T6_nbs_scorecard.justification: Abd-el-Kader et al. (2023) identify WH and flood mitigation as simultaneous spatial objectives in arid regions. Al-Hasani et al. (2023) quantify flood regulation benefits explicitly. Ejegu & Yegizaw (2020) model flood susceptibility as both a hazard to structures and a co-benefit driver for WH siting.

T6_nbs_scorecard.effect_mechanism: WH structures require upfront investment in earthworks, masonry, or lining materials. Costs range from near-zero for simple contour bunds using community labour, to significant engineering costs for check dams with concrete spillways or lined farm ponds. Unlike agroforestry, there are no ongoing input costs for tree seedlings or maintenance equivalent — the primary cost is construction.
T6_nbs_scorecard.conditionality: Costs are highly variable by structure type. Government subsidy schemes in India (MGNREGS) and Ethiopia significantly reduce effective smallholder costs. Remote locations increase material transport costs substantially.

economic_value_range.source_note: Low: community labour contour bunds (~$50/ha). High: engineered farm ponds with liners and spillways (~$800/ha). Ibrahim et al. (2019) apply explicit cost-minimisation in dam site selection. Terencio et al. (2017) calculate EUR/m3 investment cost ratios for RWH in Portugal.

T6_nbs_scorecard.justification: Ibrahim et al. (2019) apply cost-minimisation as a decision rule for dam site selection, explicitly minimising dam cross-section length to reduce costs. Terencio et al. (2017) estimate capital and O&M costs per m3 of storage. Ahmed et al. (2023) monetise ecosystem-service benefits in USD to construct a cost-benefit narrative. [archetype: Quick_returns archetype: upfront construction cost recovered within 1-3 seasons through improved yield stability. No long payback period unlike long_horizon agroforestry investments.]

sections.Sources & Databases Queried:
### 1. OpenAlex (Scholarly Literature)
Disjoined searches in Title Fields (`display_name.search`) incorporating practice synonyms and hazard-mitigation terms across English, Spanish, French, and Portuguese:

*   **Query 1 (Drought / Heat Stress)**:
    - *Filter 1 (Practices)*: `display_name.search:agroforestry|alley-cropping|silvopasture|FMNR|shade-tree|homegarden|sistemas-agroforestales|silvopastoril|agroforesterie`
    - *Filter 2 (Hazards)*: `display_name.search:drought|microclimate|shade|shading|canopy|temperature-buffer|soil-moisture|sequia|microclima|secheresse|microclimat|seca`
    - *Results*: 15 works
*   **Query 2 (Floods / Waterlogging)**:
    - *Filter 1 (Practices)*: `display_name.search:agroforestry|alley-cropping|silvopasture|vegetative-buffer|contour-buffer|sistemas-agroforestales|système-agroforestier|brise-vent`
    - *Filter 2 (Hazards)*: `display_name.search:flood|flooding|runoff|hydrology|hydrological|infiltration|water-retention|waterlogging|inundacion|escurrimiento|infiltracion|inondation|ruissellement|encharcamento`
    - *Results*: 15 works
*   **Query 3 (Wind / Storms)**:
    - *Filter 1 (Practices)*: `display_name.search:agroforestry|windbreak|shelterbelt|live-fence|hedgerow|cortinas-rompevientos|barreras-rompevientos|cercas-vivas|brise-vent|quebra-ventos`
    - *Filter 2 (Hazards)*: `display_name.search:wind|shelter|erosion|protection|storm|cyclone|viento|tormenta|vent|tempete|vento|tempestade`
    - *Results*: 15 works
*   **Query 4 (Erosion / Landslides)**:
    - *Filter 1 (Practices)*: `display_name.search:agroforestry|alley-cropping|vegetative-buffer|contour-buffer|tree-retention|hedgerow|sistemas-agroforestales|système-agroforestier`
    - *Filter 2 (Hazards)*: `display_name.search:erosion|landslide|slope|slopes|root|anchorage|binding|shear-strength|slope-stability|deslizamiento|pendiente|glissement-de-terrain|pente|deslizamento|declividade`
    - *Results*: 15 works
*   **Query 5 (Wildfires / Fire)**:
    - *Filter 1 (Practices)*: `display_name.search:agroforestry|alley-cropping|silvopasture|FMNR|shade-tree|sistemas-agroforestales|silvopastoril|agroforesterie`
    - *Filter 2 (Hazards)*: `display_name.search:fire|wildfire|flammability|fuel-load|incendio|feu|fogo`
    - *Results*: 10 works
*   **Query 6 (Meta-Analysis & Systematic Review Stream)**:
    - *Filter 1 (Practices)*: `display_name.search:agroforestry|alley-cropping|silvopasture|shade-tree`
    - *Filter 2 (Study Types)*: `display_name.search:meta-analysis|systematic-review|evidence-map|review`
    - *Filter 3 (Keywords)*: `display_name.search:adaptation|resilience|mitigation|productivity|benefits`
    - *Results*: 10 additional works (specifically targeting general synthesis papers that miss hazard-specific title indexing)

### 2. Targeted Institutional Database Interrogations
Structured institutional portals were queried directly to find official guides, project documents, and datasets:

*   **WOCAT SLM Database (wocat.net)**:
    - *Search Method*: Filtered the Global Database by Technology Group = `Agroforestry` AND Climate Change Adaptation benefits = `Drought / Waterlogging / Wind / Soil Erosion`.
    - *Results*: Identified specific SLM technology records detailing biophysical thresholds, establishing cost ranges, and hazard reduction ratings.
*   **FAO TECA Portal (teca.apps.fao.org)**:
    - *Search Method*: Queried the Technologies and Practices for Small Agricultural Producers portal for `agroforestry hazard mitigation` and `sloping agricultural land technology (SALT)`.
    - *Results*: Retrieved the FAO field practitioner technical guide and farm disaster risk mitigation manuals.
*   **World Bank Documents & Reports (documents.worldbank.org)**:
    - *Search Method*: Searched the project repository for sector = `Agricultural and Rural Development` AND keyword = `agroforestry` AND hazard = `drought / flood`.
    - *Results*: Retrieved Project Appraisal Documents (PADs) and disaster-screening guidelines (PROFOR-DRM).
*   **Center for Agroforestry (centerforagroforestry.org)**:
    - *Search Method*: Searched for `applied agroforestry training manual` and `riparian buffer design`.
    - *Results*: Retrieved the design guides and financial decision-support spreadsheets.

### 3. General Web, Repository & Toolkit Searches
General search tools and global meta-directories were interrogated to identify standalone software packages, code repositories, and tools hosted outside institutional databases:

*   **Nature-Positive Agrifood Systems Toolkit (agrifood-systems-toolkit.panda.org)**:
    - *Search Method*: Queried for `agroforestry` tools under "All Tools".
    - *Results*: Retrieved 4 relevant tools: FAO/UNDP NAP forestry guidelines, USAID AFOLU Carbon Calculator, CGIAR Gender and Inclusion Toolbox, and ICRAF REDD Abacus SP.
*   **General Web Search (Google / GitHub)**:
    - *Search Method*: Queried Google and GitHub for `agroforestry mapping modeling tool OR package OR repository` to find standalone software.
    - *Results*: Discovered 5 specialized tools and models: FarmTree Platform, Agroforestry Designer Toolkit (The Land App), RegenWorks, Agroforestry Design Tool (AgroforestryX), and AgroForstRechner.

sections.PRISMA-lite Funnel Counts:
| Funnel Stage | Count | Notes / Criteria |
|---|---:|---|
| **Returned (raw)** | **95** | Cumulative returns across academic disjoined OpenAlex queries, WWF toolkit search, and general web searches. |
| **Topic & Scope Filter** | **62** | Screened out urban forestry, non-agroforestry biology, and general restoration papers. |

### 2. Targeted Institutional Database Interrogations
Structured institutional portals were queried directly to find official guides, project documents, and datasets:

    - *Search Method*: Filtered the Global Database by Technology Group = `Agroforestry` AND Climate Change Adaptation benefits = `Drought / Waterlogging / Wind / Soil Erosion`.

*   **FAO TECA Portal (teca.apps.fao.org)**:
    - *Search Method*: Queried the Technologies and Practices for Small Agricultural Producers portal for `agroforestry hazard mitigation` and `sloping agricultural land technology (SALT)`.
    - *Results*: Retrieved the FAO field practitioner technical guide and farm disaster risk mitigation manuals.
*   **World Bank Documents & Reports (documents.worldbank.org)**:
    - *Search Method*: Searched the project repository for sector = `Agricultural and Rural Development` AND keyword = `agroforestry` AND hazard = `drought / flood`.
    - *Results*: Retrieved Project Appraisal Documents (PADs) and disaster-screening guidelines (PROFOR-DRM).

    - *Search Method*: Searched for `applied agroforestry training manual` and `riparian buffer design`.
    - *Results*: Retrieved the design guides and financial decision-support spreadsheets.

### 3. General Web, Repository & Toolkit Searches
General search tools and global meta-directories were interrogated to identify standalone software packages, code repositories, and tools hosted outside institutional databases:

- **EXTRACTED via OA copy:** *Quantification of Land Potential for Scaling Agroforestry in South Asia* (`10568/113409`) — **metadata-only on CGSpace** (no ORIGINAL bitstream; full text behind the Springer DOI 10.1007/s42489-020-00045-0), BUT OpenAlex/Unpaywall flagged it **hybrid OA, CC-BY** → fetched the Springer OA PDF (`source_id=cgspace_singh_southasia_2020`). **5 EV merged:** HWSD soil class 1-4 suitable / 5-7 not (cited Fischer 2008 + paper-own), FAO-LCCS land-cover class boundary, composite-index result (69% ≥55% suitable), observed tree-cover distribution (AF opportunity signal). `claim_basis` mixes `cited_secondary` (GAEZ/HWSD class defs) + `modelled`/`table`. **Gap:** Table 2 (per-variable weights — slope/precip/temp/soil/land-cover) is a garbled table, not text-extractable (needs OCR/table parse); slope/precip/temp are otherwise only dataset-described (off-scope) so skipped. Data and methods… topography of the study site was characterized… slope maps generated using DEM"), not AF suitability *rules*. sections.Sources & databases queried:
Six discovery lenses (parallel), all title-anchored / authority-weighted, executed 2026-07-17:

1. **OpenAlex REST API — T4 suitability.** `title.search` (display_name) on FMNR/ANR/RNA synonyms (EN/FR) × biophysical & land-condition terms (rainfall, aridity, soil, degradation, parkland, slope), sorted by citations.
2. **OpenAlex — T3 climate-hazard response.** FMNR/ANR/RNA × drought / climate-resilience / regreening-drought-Sahel.
3. **OpenAlex — T6 outcomes + cost.** FMNR/ANR/RNA × yield / adoption / income / tree-density / carbon / biodiversity / cost.
4. **Grey literature (authority orgs).** WebSearch of CRS, WRI, World Agroforestry/ICRAF, FAO, Regreening Africa, ELD/GIZ, World Vision, IUCN for downloadable technical guidance / MEL / economic reports.
5. **WOCAT SLM Technologies database** — FMNR / ANR technology entries (LMIC-grounded establishment conditions + benefits).
6. **Seed backward/forward citation** — canonical FMNR literature (Reij & Garrity 2016, Weston 2015, Binam 2015 & 2017, Chomba 2020, Sendzimir 2011, Haglund 2011, Garrity 2010), confirmed via OpenAlex.

**Multilingual:** title-search included EN (“farmer managed natural regeneration”, “assisted natural regeneration”) + FR (“régénération naturelle assistée”, RNA). Two FR Sahel sources included (ijbcs Mali adoption; ESJ RNA×millet).

## Gaps / next iteration

TOOL process is the main gap: no open repo with a terracing-specific code branch exposing hardcoded slope/soil/runoff reclassify tables (SWAT+SCS-CN+AHP/weighted-overlay recur as published methods, not pinnable commits; only GitHub hit is urban-tree stormwater, out of scope). A dedicated GitHub/GEE-script search is needed to find a repo where terracing is a real parameterised criterion, then pin commit sha + file:line. OpenAlex recent-title set is heavily polluted by archaeology/heritage/fluvial 'terrace' papers, so GIS-terrace-suitability siting lit is thinner than raw counts suggest and leans on WebSearch supplements. LMIC coverage strong for E.Africa (Ethiopia/Tigray stone bunds) and MENA (Yemen, Negev, Iraq) but light for Sahel/West-Africa terracing and South-Asia bench terraces beyond the Betwa India lead. WOCAT SLM records are a high-value LMIC-grounded lead needing specific technology-record URLs + snapshots before extraction. Adoption studies carry mixed T4/M2b content: extract slope/soil (T4) only, route tenure/labour/credit determinants to M2b operational_risk. No expert-opinion (Namita Task H) inputs sought this pass.
